newsitem.title: USA: Drug aids effectiveness of prostate cancer therapy.
newsitem.headline: Drug aids effectiveness of prostate cancer therapy.

text.p: Combining radiation with a drug that reduces the levels of the hormone testosterone can help men with prostate cancer survive longer, an international team of doctors concluded in Thursday's New England Journal of Medicine.
The technique "would appear to be the new standard treatment for men with locally advanced prostate cancer," said the study's co-author Dr. Padraig Warde of Princess Margaret Hospital in Ontario.

The eight-year study involved 415 men whose tumours in the walnut-size prostate gland had spread to nearby lymph nodes but no further. Researchers gave one group just radiation therapy, the usual treatment for patients with locally advanced prostate cancer, while a second group was given the radation therapy and the drug goserelin, sold under the brand name Zoladex and supplied by Zeneca-Pharma, part of Wilmington, Del.-based Zeneca Group.
Prostate tumours are sensitive to testosterone, secreted by the testicles. Goserelin produces chemical castration. Unlike surgical castration, the effects are reversable.

The researchers found that the drug-radiation combination produced an estimated five-year survival rate of 79 percent versus 62 percent for volunteers in the radiation group, an increase of 17 percent.

Among the surviving men, 85 percent were free of cancer after five years, compared with a 48 percent disease-free survival rate for volunteers who received radiation alone, according to the team, led by Dr. Michel Bolla of the University Hospital in Grenoble, France.
The drug, which was given every four weeks beginning with the first day of radiation therapy, produced some side effects.
Nearly two out of three men experienced hot flashes, and one-third of those had three or more hot flashes per day. Patients receiving the drug were also more likely to experience incontinence.
The researchers did not systematically look at impotence levels in the volunteers, whose ages ranged from 51 to 80.

Prostate cancer is diagnosed in about 244,000 Americans each year. About 40,400 men die from it annually. In most cases, doctors simply monitor the progress of the tumour because it usually grows so slowly that the patient will die of something else before prostate cancer becomes a problem.
Its initial symptoms include frequent urination or blood in the urine.
